title: The Critical Bible: Enlightenment Readers and Their Heirs
subtitle: Spinoza's new method, the Reimarus fragments and Lessing's ditch, Strauss and the category of myth, Wellhausen's documents, Schweitzer's verdict on the lives of Jesus, the fundamentalist answer, and Hans Frei on the eclipse of the Bible's own story.

sections.title: The Text Becomes an Object
sections.body:
For most of Christian history, the question a reader brought to the Bible was what God was saying through it. The reader stood inside the text's world. Its story of creation, fall, Israel, Christ and the coming kingdom was the frame in which every other story, including the reader's own, found its place. Between the middle of the seventeenth century and the late twentieth, Western scholarship learned to ask a different question first: what actually happened, and how did this text come to be? The Bible became an object of study in the way any ancient document is, to be dated, dissected and explained by causes that lay behind it.

That shift produced a discipline of extraordinary learning and a crisis of extraordinary depth. It taught the church things about its Scriptures that it had not known and could not honestly unlearn. It also carried, under the banner of neutral method, a set of convictions about the world that were never neutral at all. Both facts have to be held at once, and most Christians have found it easier to hold one or the other. The liberal tended to accept the method and its assumptions together. The fundamentalist tended to reject them together. Neither sorted the gains from the freight.

A man who came to faith from atheism, as I did, cannot treat the critic's questions as idle. They were the questions of serious people who wanted to know whether the thing was true, and some of them paid dearly for asking. But I also pastor a church whose people read the Bible, usually without knowing it, through lenses ground in this period by both sides of its argument. To understand how criticism read the Bible is to understand how we read it now. The story runs from a lens grinder in Amsterdam to a theologian at Yale who, three centuries later, named what had been lost.

sections.title: Spinoza and the Bible as Natural History
sections.body:
Benedict de Spinoza had been expelled from the Portuguese Jewish community of Amsterdam in 1656, and he earned part of his living grinding lenses. In 1670 he published, anonymously and under a false imprint, the Theological-Political Treatise. Its political aim was the freedom to philosophize within a republic, and its means of securing that freedom was a new way of reading Scripture. The interpretation of Scripture, Spinoza argued, should proceed as the interpretation of nature does, by first assembling a history of the text: its language, the lives and purposes of its authors, the occasions of its writing, the way it was collected and handed down. Meaning was to be established from that history alone, and kept strictly apart from the question of whether what the text said was true.

The consequences were drastic. Following hints in the medieval Jewish commentator Abraham ibn Ezra, Spinoza argued that Moses did not write the Pentateuch, and he assigned the historical books to a single later compiler, probably Ezra. Miracles, in his system, were impossible in principle, since the laws of nature were nothing other than God's own necessary decrees; a reported miracle was an event whose natural cause its witnesses did not grasp. Prophecy was vivid imagination put to moral use. Scripture existed to teach obedience and justice to people who could not reach the truth by reason, and it should not be asked for philosophy.

Spinoza was not alone. Thomas Hobbes had already questioned Mosaic authorship in Leviathan in 1651, and in 1678 the French Oratorian priest Richard Simon published a Critical History of the Old Testament that described a long process of editing, partly in order to show Protestants that Scripture could not be read without the church's tradition. But it was Spinoza who set the terms. The text's meaning was one question and its truth another, and the reader's reason sat as judge of the second.

sections.title: The Fragments and the Ugly Ditch
sections.body:
Hermann Samuel Reimarus taught oriental languages at the academic gymnasium in Hamburg and lived as a respectable Lutheran. In private he spent years writing a defense of rational religion that rejected revealed religion altogether, and he never published it. After his death in 1768, Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, then librarian to the Duke of Brunswick at Wolfenbüttel, released portions of the manuscript between 1774 and 1778 as fragments by an unnamed author, presenting them as finds from the ducal library.

The last and most explosive of them, on the aims of Jesus and his disciples, proposed that Jesus had been a Jewish messianic claimant who expected a political kingdom, that his cry of dereliction on the cross marked the collapse of that hope, and that his disciples, unwilling to go back to their nets, took the body and invented the resurrection and a spiritual redemption in place of the kingdom that never came. It was a crude theory. Its importance lay in the line it drew between the Jesus of history and the Christ the church proclaimed, a line that would organize two centuries of scholarship.

Lessing did not adopt Reimarus's conclusions, but he drew from the controversy a principle that proved more durable than the fragments. In an essay of 1777 he argued that accidental truths of history can never become the proof of necessary truths of reason, and he called the gap between them an ugly, broad ditch that he could not get across, however earnestly he tried to leap. The image named a whole culture's anxiety. If faith rested on events, and events could be known only with probability, faith seemed to rest on sand. The Enlightenment's answer was to move religion's foundation out of history and into reason or moral feeling, where no historian could reach it. The question of what actually happened in Jerusalem did not go away. It was simply declared beside the point.

sections.title: Strauss and the Category of Myth
sections.body:
David Friedrich Strauss was twenty-seven and a tutor at the Protestant seminary in Tübingen when he published The Life of Jesus, Critically Examined, in two volumes in 1835 and 1836. He accepted neither of the two readings of the Gospels then in possession of the field. The supernaturalists took the miracle stories as reports of events that happened as described. The rationalists, Heinrich Paulus prominent among them, took them as reports of natural events misunderstood, so that Jesus walked on the shore rather than the sea. Strauss thought both had mistaken the kind of writing in front of them. The Gospel narratives, he argued, were largely myth, the unconscious creation of the early communities rather than deliberate fraud, which clothed their conviction that Jesus was the Messiah in stories drawn from Israel's Scriptures and hopes.

The book was a sensation and a scandal. Strauss lost his post at Tübingen, and when Zurich called him to a chair in 1839, popular uproar kept him from ever taking it up. In 1846 Mary Ann Evans, later known to the world as the novelist George Eliot, published an English translation, and the book entered the bloodstream of Victorian unbelief.

His lasting contribution was the question of genre. He was right that a reader must ask what kind of writing a text is before deciding what it claims, and right that the Gospels are shaped at every turn by the Scriptures of Israel. Where he erred was in deciding beforehand that any narrative of divine action must be myth because such action does not occur. That was not a finding of his method. It was its premise. In The Old Faith and the New of 1872 Strauss concluded that he was no longer a Christian and that the scientific view of the world had taken the faith's place. He was more honest than many of his admirers about where the premise led.

sections.title: Wellhausen and the Documents Behind the Law
sections.body:
Criticism of the Old Testament followed a parallel course. In 1753 the French physician Jean Astruc observed that Genesis alternates between two names for God and proposed that Moses had worked from earlier documents. Over the following century German scholars refined the observation into a theory of written sources, and Julius Wellhausen gave it its classic form. His history of Israel appeared in 1878 and was reissued in 1883 as the Prolegomena to the History of Israel, and its argument governed Old Testament scholarship for much of a century.

The documentary hypothesis, as Wellhausen framed it, held that the Pentateuch had been woven from four principal sources, lettered J, E, D and P, composed over several centuries. The decisive move concerned the priestly material. Building on the work of Karl Heinrich Graf, Wellhausen argued that the elaborate priestly legislation came after the great prophets rather than before them, in the period of the exile and the return. The law, in this reconstruction, was the late codification of a religion that had once been spontaneous and prophetic and had hardened into ritual. Israel's history ran from vitality to legalism.

The analysis was brilliant, and some of its observations about the composite character of the Pentateuch have outlived the scheme that organized them. Yet its story of decline from free prophetic faith to priestly law resembled a liberal Protestant's account of his own history, in which a free gospel had been smothered by Catholic ritual, and later scholars have recognized how entangled its disdain for the law was with a disdain for Judaism. Wellhausen was candid about where his work had left him. In 1882 he resigned his chair in theology at Greifswald, explaining that he had come to theology for the scientific study of the Bible and had realized that, despite his restraint, he was unfitting his students for the ministry. He spent the rest of his career in Semitic philology.

sections.title: Schweitzer and the Face in the Well
sections.body:
By the opening of the twentieth century the lives of Jesus filled a long shelf, and in 1906 a young Strasbourg scholar reviewed it. Albert Schweitzer's From Reimarus to Wrede, published in English in 1910 as The Quest of the Historical Jesus, is one of the few works of biblical scholarship that reads as a verdict on an age. His finding was devastating. Each epoch, he observed, had found its own reflection in Jesus, and each writer had tended to create him in accordance with his own character. The rationalists found a teacher of reason, the romantics a religious genius, the liberals an ethical teacher of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man.

The Catholic Modernist George Tyrrell made the same point with an image a few years later. The Christ whom Adolf von Harnack saw, Tyrrell wrote in substance, was only the reflection of a liberal Protestant face glimpsed at the bottom of a deep well. Harnack's lectures of 1899 and 1900, published as What Is Christianity?, had distilled the gospel into the fatherhood of God, the infinite value of the human soul and the higher righteousness of the commandment of love. It was a gospel a cultivated Berliner could hold without embarrassment.

Schweitzer's own reconstruction was an apocalyptic prophet who expected the end of the world, laid hold of the wheel of history to turn it toward its close, and was crushed by it. That figure was strange to modern people, and Schweitzer meant him to be. The point of the book was that the historical Jesus, honestly sought, refuses to be domesticated. Schweitzer then left the lecture hall, qualified in medicine, and in 1913 went to Lambaréné in French Equatorial Africa to run a hospital, the work of most of his remaining life. Whatever one makes of his theology, he would not let Jesus remain a mirror. Few of his readers have managed as much.

sections.title: The Defenders and What They Shared
sections.body:
The churches did not receive criticism quietly. At Princeton Seminary, Charles Hodge and then Benjamin B. Warfield built a careful doctrine of Scripture whose classic statement, an article on inspiration by A. A. Hodge and Warfield in 1881, argued that the Bible as originally given was free from error in all that it affirms. Between 1910 and 1915 The Fundamentals carried a popular defense of the faith's foundations, the trustworthiness of Scripture among them, into churches across America. Rome answered too. In 1907 Pope Pius X condemned Modernism in the encyclical Pascendi, and Catholic critical scholarship lived under suspicion for a generation.

The defenders were right about what was at stake. A method that ruled out divine action in advance could not be reconciled with the creeds by adjusting its conclusions, because the conflict lay in its premises. Mark Noll has shown that evangelical scholars engaged criticism with more learning than their caricature allows. But the same historians have noticed something the defenders did not. The Princeton doctrine rested heavily on Scottish common sense philosophy, and it treated the Bible, in the manner associated with Francis Bacon, as a storehouse of facts to be arranged like a scientist's data. The fundamentalist and the critic disagreed about the facts. They agreed, largely, that the meaning of a biblical narrative was the fact it referred to.

Some answers moved past defense. Pius XII's encyclical Divino Afflante Spiritu in 1943 encouraged Catholic scholars to study the Bible's literary forms, and the Second Vatican Council's constitution Dei Verbum in 1965 taught that God speaks in Scripture through human authors in human fashion, so that the interpreter must attend to their forms of writing and read within the living faith of the whole church. Rome, which had resisted criticism longest, found a way to receive its gains without surrendering the creed, perhaps because it had never asked the solitary reader to carry the whole weight.

sections.title: The Eclipse, and What It Leaves Us
sections.body:
In 1974 Hans Frei, a theologian teaching at Yale, published The Eclipse of Biblical Narrative, naming what three centuries of argument had obscured. Precritical readers, Frei argued, took the Bible's realistic narratives as the one true story of the world and fitted their own lives and times into it. Through the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries that order reversed. The meaning of the narrative came to be located behind or beyond it, in a historical event to be confirmed or denied, or in a moral and religious idea to be extracted. Critics and defenders alike asked chiefly whether the story was factual. Fewer asked what it would mean to live inside it. Michael Legaspi has since shown how the eighteenth-century German university, at Göttingen above all, fashioned an academic Bible for a post-confessional state, studied with the tools of classical philology, while the scriptural Bible of the churches receded.

The critics' gains are real, and the church should name them without grudging. Hermann Gunkel's attention to literary form, the Babylonian tablets George Smith presented in 1872, and the Dead Sea Scrolls found from 1947, some of them about a thousand years older than the medieval manuscripts the Hebrew text had rested on, taught us that God spoke through human authors in real genres, real languages and real histories. A pastor who ignores that does his people no honor.

But the method carried a world with it. Charles Taylor has described the buffered self, sealed against any power beyond the natural order, and the immanent frame in which that order runs on its own. Criticism often presented that frame as a finding when it was an assumption. The deeper loss reached all of us, liberal and fundamentalist alike, for we learned to stand outside the Bible as an object to be verified or debunked. My own study holds both shelves. What remains is whether we can still let the text read us.

keyFigures.name: Benedict de Spinoza
keyFigures.note: Dutch philosopher whose Theological-Political Treatise of 1670 proposed reading Scripture as one reads nature.

keyFigures.name: Hermann Samuel Reimarus
keyFigures.note: Hamburg scholar whose unpublished attack on revelation became the fragments Lessing released from 1774 to 1778.

keyFigures.name: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing
keyFigures.note: Dramatist and critic who published the fragments and named the ugly, broad ditch between history and reason.

keyFigures.name: David Friedrich Strauss
keyFigures.note: Tübingen tutor whose Life of Jesus of 1835 read the Gospels as myth and cost him his career.

keyFigures.name: Julius Wellhausen
keyFigures.note: Scholar whose Prolegomena of 1883 gave the documentary hypothesis its classic form.

keyFigures.name: Albert Schweitzer
keyFigures.note: Scholar, physician and organist whose Quest of the Historical Jesus showed each life of Jesus mirroring its author.

keyFigures.name: Hans Frei
keyFigures.note: Yale theologian whose Eclipse of Biblical Narrative of 1974 showed how meaning moved behind the text.
